name: Seaweed
lede: Seaweed is a vivid emerald-leaning green on screen, but the books use the word for something duller: the yellowish green and olive of the real thing.

sections.title: Two seaweeds
sections.body: Paterson defines seaweed green as a yellowish green [1], and lists it among the greens beside sea-green and sap green [2]. The swatch here is far more vivid than that: the xkcd survey's Seaweed, #18D17B, is a saturated mint-emerald with a measured chroma of 69 [3]. This is a case where the name and the screen color disagree, and the dictionary sense is the safer guide to the plant [1][3].

sections.title: The color of a faded robe
sections.body: Finlay describes how Michelangelo's *The Entombment* uses azurite, a copper-mine blue, for Mary Magdalene's robe, which has since faded from sea blue to a seaweed-like, unflattering olive [4]. Azurite leans toward green, which Finlay credits for both the sea-like blue and the later shift [4]. St Clair describes the archil lichens that dye used as a buff-grey growing in clumps that look like pale seaweed [5].

sections.title: Pigments of seaweeds
sections.body: The real thing carries many pigments. Paterson lists phycophaein, a reddish-brown pigment found in certain seaweeds, and phycoxanthin, a yellow one [6]. Paterson ties the Red Sea's name to a red algal pigment, phycoerythrin (*phyco* for alga, *eryth* for red); that etymology is not settled [6]. Baty notes a hair-brown shade visible on the fucus seaweed in a 1737 botanical plate by Weinmann [7]. Seaweed also mattered to glassmakers, since sodium-rich seaweed was a natural source of flux [8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The only source for the swatch is xkcd; its nearest named color is [[emerald]], at a color distance (ΔE) of 3.4, and it sits in the greens [3]. No painting in the ColorHub archive of 23,531 carries a color this close, as photographed [9]. Related: [[seaweed-green]], [[sea-green]] and [[green]].
